passage: Jomon, you're going to be a prefect, so let Seema Miss tell you about one boy from my years as a teacher. His name was Tenzin, and he had been making fake posts about a girl called Shruti. When it came out, the school suspended him for a week. But I also sat with him. I asked, "What did you get from this?" He said his friends only noticed him when he was being mean. We found him a counsellor, and he helped with the school magazine after that. He wrote Shruti a real apology. Shruti had counselling too, and she joined the debate club again. And the whole class had to talk honestly about who had watched and done nothing.

qa.q: How long was Tenzin suspended?
qa.a: He was suspended for a week.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin say he made the posts?
qa.a: He said his friends only noticed him when he was being mean, which suggests he wanted attention and belonging.

qa.q: What can Jomon learn from Seema Miss about repair?
qa.a: Real repair has several parts: a clear consequence for the boy, help for what drives him, support for the target, and a class that faces its own silence.

qa.q: How might Shruti feel as she rejoins the debate club?
qa.a: She may feel nervous but more confident, knowing the school took her side and she had support.

grounding: It shows a boy facing consequences and support to understand harm, the target regaining confidence, and bystanders learning silence costs something.

passage: The school hall's fans had broken in the heat, and the class meeting had only twenty minutes before the next period. The boy who had been posting cruel comments about Deepika had already been dealt with by the school, and he was seeing the counsellor every week. Now it was the class's turn. The teacher asked, "How many of you saw the posts?" Almost every hand went up. "How many said anything?" Two hands. Farida was one of them. The silence felt heavy. Deepika sat by the window, beside Farida, her head up this time. After weeks of sessions with the counsellor, she had started drawing again. When the bell rang, three classmates walked over to Deepika and said sorry for staying quiet.

qa.q: How many hands went up when the teacher asked who said anything?
qa.a: Two hands went up, and Farida was one of them.

qa.q: What does Deepika sitting with her head up suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she is feeling more confident and safe again after weeks of counselling and support.

qa.q: Why was the class meeting an important part of repair?
qa.a: It helped the whole class see that staying silent allowed the harm, which led three classmates to apologise and may make them act sooner next time.

qa.q: How might the classmates who stayed silent feel after the meeting?
qa.a: They likely feel uncomfortable and a bit guilty, realising their silence had a cost for Deepika.

grounding: It illustrates the bully facing consequences with support, the target regaining confidence, and the bystanders learning that silence has a cost.

passage:
The meeting in the counsellor's room at the Lucknow school lasted an hour. Jasleen sat on one side, arms crossed. Salma sat on the other, next to her mother.

Jasleen had already been suspended for a week for the posts she made about Salma. Today was the other part.

The counsellor asked Jasleen to read aloud three of her own posts. Halfway through the second one, Jasleen's voice cracked. "I didn't think... it looks different read out loud."

Salma said quietly, "I stopped going to dance class because of these."

Jasleen looked at her for the first time. "I'm sorry. I did it because the group laughed. I wanted them to like me." The counsellor arranged weekly sessions for Jasleen to talk about that.

Two weeks later, Salma went back to dance class. Her friends went with her. And in the class chat, when someone started a new joke about another girl, three people typed, "Not again. Stop."

qa.q: How long had Jasleen been suspended?
qa.a: For a week.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel when she read her posts aloud?
qa.a: Her voice cracked; she felt ashamed, realising how cruel the posts looked read out loud.

qa.q: How did this process help both girls and the class?
qa.a: Jasleen faced consequences, understood the harm and got counselling for her need for approval; Salma got support to return to dance; the class learned to speak up instead of staying silent.

qa.q: How might Salma feel hearing Jasleen's apology?
qa.a: She may feel some relief and a little more confident, seeing Jasleen understand the harm.

grounding: After consequences, Jasleen faces the harm of her posts in a counselling meeting and gets support, while Salma regains confidence and the class learns silence has a cost.

passage:
"Sudha, you asked to talk. Ms Kurian says I don't have to."

"I know, Jahnavi. You don't. I just... I read the messages again. The ones I sent in March."

"And?"

"They were horrible. I told myself they were jokes. They weren't."

"I stopped eating lunch at school because of them."

"I know. Ms Kurian told me. I'm sorry."

"Why did you do it?"

"Because when I made fun of you, Tanvi's group laughed and let me sit with them. I didn't have anyone else."

"...That's sad. It doesn't make it okay."

"I know it doesn't. I lost my place on the student council. I deserved that. I'm seeing the counsellor every week."

"I'm still angry."

"You can be."

"But I'm eating lunch again. Asha and Liza sit with me. They didn't when it started. Now they say they should have."

qa.q: What did Sudha lose because of the messages?
qa.a: Her place on the student council.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi feel during this conversation?
qa.a: Jahnavi is still angry, but is also steadier and more confident, eating lunch again with friends.

qa.q: What makes this repair meaningful?
qa.a: Sudha accepts the consequence, names the harm without excuses, and gets counselling for what drove her, while Jahnavi has support and the right to stay angry.

qa.q: What did Asha and Liza learn, according to Jahnavi?
qa.a: That staying silent at the start was wrong; they now say they should have sat with Jahnavi sooner.

grounding: In a supervised talk Sudha faces consequences, owns the harm and gets help for her need to belong, while Jahnavi regains confidence and bystanders see silence's cost.

passage:
I was one of the people who watched Lokesh bully Anish for most of Class 10 and said nothing. I'm Manjula, and this is how it ended.

When Anish's mother finally went to the principal with the screenshots, the school acted fast. Lokesh was suspended and had to meet Anish with the counsellor. He also had to attend sessions about why he did it. I heard later his older brother had been bullying him at home for years.

Anish got counselling too. By the end of term he was back in the quiz team, and he started laughing in class again.

But what I remember most is the assembly afterwards. The principal read out, anonymously, what it felt like to be Anish. Then she said, "Every one of you who saw and said nothing helped it go on." I felt my face go hot. She was talking about me.

I haven't stayed silent since.

qa.q: What team did Anish return to by the end of term?
qa.a: The quiz team.

qa.q: How did Manjula feel at the assembly?
qa.a: Manjula felt ashamed, face hot, realising that silence had helped the bullying go on.

qa.q: What did the school do for both Lokesh and Anish?
qa.a: It gave Lokesh consequences and sessions to understand the harm and what drove it, and gave Anish counselling so he could regain his confidence.

qa.q: How might Anish have felt as he returned to the quiz team?
qa.a: He was probably relieved and more confident, starting to feel like himself again.

grounding: Manjula, a bystander, recalls Lokesh facing consequences and help, Anish recovering with support, and the class learning that silence has a cost.

passage: Counsellor's note, end of term. Six weeks since the incidents involving Ramesh and Lokesh in Class 9. Ramesh served his suspension and has attended five of six sessions with me. Early on he shrugged: "It was just a joke." Two weeks ago I read him, without names, what Lokesh had written about lying awake before school. Ramesh went very quiet and asked if he could write to Lokesh. He also spoke for the first time about the pressure at home to be "the strong one". Lokesh has been meeting me weekly as well. Last Friday he presented his science model to the whole class, his voice shaking at first, then steady. In yesterday's class circle, several students admitted they had seen it and said nothing. One girl said, "Next time I won't just watch." I will keep both boys' check-ins going next term.

qa.q: How many sessions has Ramesh attended?
qa.a: Ramesh has attended five of six sessions.

qa.q: What does Ramesh going quiet after hearing Lokesh's words suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he finally felt the weight of the harm, perhaps ashamed or remorseful, since he then asked to write to Lokesh.

qa.q: What made this repair more than just punishment?
qa.a: Ramesh got a consequence plus sessions to understand the harm and his own pressure at home, Lokesh got weekly support, and the class reflected on staying silent.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt presenting the science model to the class?
qa.a: Lokesh was probably nervous at first, with a shaking voice, then steadier and likely proud as his confidence returned.

grounding: Shows a student who bullied facing consequences and a chance to understand the harm, the target regaining confidence, and bystanders learning that silence has a cost.
